title: Reading a receipt like a detective
description: A receipt is a tiny crime-scene report of your spending: quantities, prices, taxes, offers — and occasionally, mistakes in the shop's favour. Learn to read one properly.

body.heading: The thirty-second scan
paragraphs: Before you leave the till, scan three things: the items you bought once but were charged for twice, the full-price item that should have been on offer, and the quantity line on anything sold by weight. Till errors are common, honest, and far easier to fix while you are still standing there.
Check the date, the total, and — if you paid by card — that the card total matches the receipt total. Two numbers that disagree are a question worth asking on the spot.

body.heading: What the small print is telling you
paragraphs: A receipt quietly records your real life: the tax you paid, the loyalty points earned, the return deadline, and sometimes a survey offer that is genuinely worth money off a future shop. The returns line matters most — many shops print the last return date right there, and it is shorter than people assume.
Photograph receipts for anything with a warranty. Paper fades; a photo in a folder called “Receipts 2026” will still be readable when the washing machine misbehaves in 2028.

body.heading: The weekly five-minute habit
paragraphs: Once a week, read one or two receipts properly and compare them with what you meant to spend. You are not auditing yourself for blame — you are collecting the facts a budget is supposed to be built from.
Most people discover the same thing: the plan in their head and the story on the paper differ by a handful of small, fixable surprises.

takeaway: Scan every receipt for double charges and missed offers before you leave the till, photograph the warranty ones, and review a couple each week.
